title: Sikkim's pilgrim trail: Char Dham to Ralang
meta_description: Char Dham, Samdruptse, Buddha Park and Ralang: what each South Sikkim pilgrim site means, how long to spend, fees, timings and a 2–3 day order that works.
summary: South Sikkim holds four of the state's best-known pilgrim sites within 40 km of each other: the Hindu Char Dham complex at Namchi, the Guru Padmasambhava statue at Samdruptse, the giant Buddha at Ravangla's Buddha Park and the Kagyu monastery at Ralang. Two unhurried days cover them; three suits seniors.

sections.heading: One small district, two faiths, many hills
paras: In most of India a pilgrim circuit means long days on the road. In Namchi district it means four major sites on a single ridge system, each between half an hour and an hour from the next. That closeness is not an accident. In the 2000s and early 2010s the Sikkim government built large pilgrim and heritage projects in the south to spread tourism beyond Gangtok and Pelling, and to honour both of the state's main religious traditions: Hindu, followed by most of the Nepali-speaking majority, and Buddhist, followed by the Bhutia, most Lepcha, and the Sherpa, Tamang and other communities.

The result is a trail where a family can do the Char Dham parikrama at dawn, eat lunch below a 135 ft statue of Guru Rinpoche, and watch evening light on a 130 ft Buddha. Respect is the same everywhere: dress modestly, walk clockwise around Buddhist shrines and stupas, take shoes off where asked, and ask before photographing monks or rituals.

sections.heading: Char Dham on Solophok hill
paras: The Siddheshwar Dham, better known as Char Dham, stands on Solophok hill about 5 km from Namchi bazaar. It was inaugurated on 8 November 2011. The centrepiece is a seated Shiva usually given as 108 ft (about 33 m) high, which you see from the road long before you arrive. Around it are replicas of the four great dhams of Hindu pilgrimage, Badrinath, Dwarka, Jagannath Puri and Rameswaram, and of the twelve jyotirlingas, so a pilgrim can complete a symbolic circuit of India in a single morning. There is also a shrine to Kirateshwar, Shiva in his form as a hunter, which carries a special meaning in Sikkim and Darjeeling, where the Kirat (Limbu and Rai) heritage is strong.

Go at opening time, roughly 8 am, when the light on the statue is soft and the platforms are quiet. Allow two to three hours. The complex is large and has a lot of steps between levels; seniors should take it slowly and rest at the covered benches. Simple vegetarian food and a pilgrim lodge are on site. Timings and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Samdruptse and Guru Rinpoche
paras: Guru Padmasambhava, called Guru Rinpoche in Sikkim, is the eighth-century teacher credited in Tibetan Buddhist tradition with bringing Vajrayana Buddhism across the Himalaya and blessing Sikkim as a beyul, a hidden sacred land. His statue at Samdruptse, about 7 km from Namchi on the ridge road, is 135 ft high and was completed in 2004; it is painted copper and gold and faces the town. Samdruptse is usually translated as wish-fulfilling hill.

As told locally, the hill was once a dormant volcano, and Buddhist monks have long offered prayers on its summit to keep it calm; treat that as local tradition rather than geology. The approach from the car park is a paved path with a few flights of steps. On clear mornings between October and April you see the Kangchenjunga range across the valleys. Combine it with Namchi Rock Garden, a terraced park on the same road, which is easy walking and has a small café.

If you have an extra hour in Namchi, visit Ngadak monastery on the edge of town. It is one of the older gompas in the south, with a newer hall built beside the original. It sees few tourists, and the monks are used to quiet visitors who walk around the prayer wheels and sit for a while. Namchi also has a Shirdi Sai Baba temple at Assangthang, popular with families from the plains.

sections.heading: Buddha Park at Ravangla
paras: Tathagata Tsal, or Buddha Park, lies about 1 km from Ravangla market, at roughly 2,100 m, within the grounds of the older Rabong monastery. The 130 ft statue of the Buddha was built between 2006 and 2013, partly to mark the 2,550th anniversary of the Buddha's birth, and was consecrated by the Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013. According to the Wikipedia article on the park, it used about 60 tonnes of copper, worked by the repoussé method.

Inside the base is a spiral gallery that tells the life of the Buddha in paintings, and the park has wide paved paths, lawns and a small lake. It is the most accessible site on the trail: almost level from the gate to the statue, with places to sit. The best time is the first hour after opening, around 9 am, and again after 4 pm when the light turns warm. Maenam hill rises behind, and on clear days the snow peaks stand to the north-west.

sections.heading: Ralang and the masked dances
paras: Ralang Monastery, Ralong Palchen Choling, is about 6 km below Ravangla. It belongs to the Kagyu school, and the monastery was established in 1768; the present large building was completed in 1995 under the 12th Gyaltsab Rinpoche, and the older Karma Rabtenling gompa still stands nearby. The main hall holds a fine collection of paintings and thangkas.

Ralang is best known for its masked dances, cham. Pang Lhabsol, when Kangchenjunga is worshipped as Sikkim's guardian deity, falls on the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month, usually late August or September. The Kagyed dances on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth month usually fall in December, and Ralang's Mahakala dances draw visitors from across the state. Dates follow the lunar calendar and move each year, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The order that works
paras: Start in Namchi and finish in Ravangla, or the reverse; both work. The Namchi sites face east and look best in morning light, the Ravangla ones in the afternoon. Namchi to Ravangla is about 26 km, an hour by car.

For most people we suggest two nights: one in Namchi, one in Ravangla. For seniors, three nights at an easy pace, with no early starts and an afternoon rest each day, makes the trip pleasant rather than tiring.
list: Day 1: arrive Namchi from Siliguri (≈ 100 km · 3.5–4 h); evening aarti or a quiet walk at Char Dham
Day 2: Char Dham at opening time, Samdruptse, Rock Garden; drive to Ravangla (≈ 26 km · 1 h)
Day 3: Buddha Park at 9 am, Ralang Monastery, optional Temi Tea Garden (≈ 20 km)
Day 4: drive back to Siliguri (≈ 125 km · 4.5–5 h) or on to Pelling or Gangtok

sections.heading: Practical notes for pilgrims
paras: No permits are needed for Indian nationals anywhere on this trail; foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online. Hotels collect the ₹50 state entry fee once per 30 days. Carry a shawl or jacket even in May: Ravangla at 2,100 m is often 10 °C cooler than Siliguri. Shops at Char Dham sell flowers and offerings; at Buddhist sites, a kata (white scarf) or a few notes in the donation box is customary. The trail is busy on Sundays and during Durga Puja and Diwali holidays, quiet on weekday mornings.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the South Sikkim pilgrim circuit?
faqs.a: Two nights covers Char Dham, Samdruptse, Buddha Park and Ralang without rushing: one night in Namchi, one in Ravangla. Three nights is better for seniors or anyone who wants to add Temi Tea Garden or a festival day. All four sites are within about 40 km of each other.

faqs.q: What is the Char Dham in Sikkim?
faqs.a: It is the Siddheshwar Dham on Solophok hill near Namchi, inaugurated in 2011. It has a seated Shiva about 108 ft (33 m) high, replicas of the four dhams (Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram) and the twelve jyotirlingas, and a Kirateshwar shrine. Pilgrims treat it as a symbolic Char Dham yatra in one place.

faqs.q: Is Char Dham Namchi suitable for elderly people?
faqs.a: Yes, at a gentle pace. The complex is large, with many steps between levels and covered places to rest. Go early, around 8 am, before the crowds and the midday sun, and allow two to three hours. A driver can drop you close to the entrance. Buddha Park at Ravangla is flatter and easier.

faqs.q: Who built the Buddha statue at Ravangla?
faqs.a: The statue at Tathagata Tsal (Buddha Park) was built by the Sikkim government between 2006 and 2013 within the Rabong monastery grounds. It stands 130 ft high and was consecrated by the Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013. A gallery inside the base tells the life of the Buddha.

faqs.q: What are the timings of Buddha Park, Ravangla?
faqs.a: The park has generally been open from about 9 am to 5.30 or 6 pm daily, with an entry fee of about ₹50 for Indians and ₹100 for foreign nationals. Timings and fees change, so check current status before you travel. The first hour after opening is the quietest.

For the 135 ft statue of Guru Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche), the patron saint of Sikkim, completed in 2004 on a ridge about 7 km from Namchi. The name is usually translated as wish-fulfilling hill. On clear mornings you also see the Kangchenjunga range from the platform.

faqs.q: When are the masked dances at Ralang Monastery?
faqs.a: Ralang holds cham dances at Pang Lhabsol, on the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month (usually late August or September), and the Kagyed and Mahakala dances on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth month, usually in December. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Char Dham or Buddha Park?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need any permit. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, which since January 2026 is applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India; it covers the South Sikkim sights. Hotels also collect a ₹50 per person state fee.

faqs.q: Can I do the pilgrim sites as a day trip from Gangtok?
faqs.a: It is possible but tiring. Gangtok to Namchi is about 3 hours each way and Ravangla adds more, so you would spend seven hours in the car for perhaps four hours at the sites. We suggest at least one night in Namchi or Ravangla.
